h1: Rent as a share of revenue and what a brewpub can afford
title: How Much Rent Can a Brewpub Afford? | Craft Beer School
desc: How to judge what rent a brewpub can afford in an Indian city: rent as a share of revenue, the hidden occupancy costs, escalations and testing the numbers.
teaser: The location is perfect and the rent is steep. The question is whether the beer can pay for it.
standfirst: Rent is one of the few big brewpub costs that is fixed from day one, busy month or quiet. Getting it wrong can sink a good brewpub. Here is how to judge what you can afford.
sections:
Most brewpub costs move with sales to some extent. Raw materials scale with volume. Staff hours can be adjusted. Rent does not move. It is due in a slow monsoon month exactly as it is in a busy December. A rent that feels manageable in a good month can be crushing in a bad one.

Brewpubs also need more space than most restaurants. The brewhouse, fermenters, cold room and grain store take floor area that earns nothing directly from guests. That makes rent per seat higher than for a restaurant of the same size.
Rent as a share of revenue

Restaurant operators often judge rent as a percentage of revenue. A rough rule of thumb many use is that total occupancy cost should stay somewhere around 10 to 15 percent of revenue, though the right figure depends on your format, prices and location. A destination brewpub with high spend per guest can carry a higher rent than a neighbourhood taproom. Treat the rule of thumb as a warning light, not a target.

The critical point: use realistic revenue, not your best-case forecast. If rent is 12 percent of your optimistic sales, it may be 20 percent of what you actually sell in year one.

Rent is only part of what the space costs. Add:

  • Maintenance or common area charges.
  • Property tax, if passed on to you.
  • Security deposit, which ties up cash for years.
  • Fit-out and structural work, especially floor strengthening, drainage and ventilation for brewing.
  • Insurance and utility connection costs.

A security deposit of many months' rent, common in Indian commercial leases, is money you cannot use for anything else. Our guide to leasing space for a brewpub covers lease terms in detail.

Indian commercial leases often include annual or periodic rent escalations and a lock-in period during which you cannot exit without paying. Model the escalations over the full lock-in. A rent that is affordable in year one can be painful by year five if sales have not grown as fast as the escalation clause.

Negotiate a rent-free period for fit-out and licensing. A brewpub can take months to get licences after the lease is signed. Paying full rent on an empty site during that time drains cash.

Some landlords, especially in malls, offer rent linked to revenue: a minimum guaranteed rent or a percentage of sales, whichever is higher. This can protect you in slow months and share the upside with the landlord in good ones. It also means the landlord sees your sales figures and may audit them. Read the definition of revenue carefully: does it include excise, service charge or events? Small wording differences can change the rent a lot.

Instead of asking whether you like the rent, ask what revenue the space must produce to carry it. Build a simple model:

  1. Estimate seats, covers per day, spend per guest and days open.
  2. Apply a realistic ramp-up for the first year.
  3. Subtract cost of goods, labour, utilities and other costs.
  4. See what is left to pay rent, debt and a return.

If the rent only works when the brewpub is full every night, the rent is too high. Our taproom economics guide shows the cost lines to include.

A cheaper site in the wrong place is no bargain. Footfall, parking, visibility, the office crowd nearby and neighbours who will not complain about noise all affect revenue. Our guide to choosing a brewery location covers what to check. Excise rules can also restrict sites near schools, temples or hospitals, which narrows your choices.

The best site is one where realistic revenue comfortably carries the full occupancy cost. Sometimes that means a less glamorous street with a much lower rent.
Walk the space with a brewer

Before you sign, walk the space with someone who has built a brewery. They will see what a property agent will not: whether the floor can take a full fermenter, where the drains are, whether the ceiling fits the tallest tank and where the grain arrives. Those details turn into fit-out cost. Fit-out cost belongs in your occupancy maths too.
faqs: What percentage of revenue should rent be for a brewpub?
Many operators use a rough guide of about 10 to 15 percent for total occupancy cost, but the right figure depends on your format and location. Test it against realistic revenue.
Why do brewpubs pay more rent per seat than restaurants?
The brewhouse, tanks and cold room take floor space that does not seat guests.
Should I negotiate a rent-free period?
Yes, if possible. Fit-out and licensing can take months. Paying rent on an empty site drains cash.
